title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Public Debts.

In the third book of this Inquiry I tried to show what happens in that primitive state of society which comes before commerce spreads and manufacturing improves. There the expensive luxuries that only commerce and manufacturing can supply are entirely unknown, and so a man with a large income has no way to spend or enjoy it except by supporting roughly as many people as that income can support. A large income, at any time, amounts to command over a large quantity of life's necessities. In that primitive state it is usually paid in those necessities themselves: in plain food and coarse clothing, in grain and cattle, in wool and raw hides. When neither commerce nor manufacturing offers anything the owner can exchange for most of these materials once his own needs are met, he can do nothing with the surplus except feed and clothe as many people as it will feed and clothe. In such conditions, the main expenses of the rich and powerful take the form of a hospitality without luxury and a generosity without show. But, as I also tried to show in the same book, these are not the kinds of expense that easily ruin a man. There is hardly any selfish pleasure, however trivial, that has not sometimes ruined even sensible men. A passion for cockfighting has ruined many. Yet I believe it is rare for people to be ruined by hospitality or generosity of this plain kind, even though the hospitality of luxury and the generosity of display have ruined many. Among our feudal ancestors, the fact that estates stayed in the same family for so long is proof enough that people generally lived within their incomes. The rough hospitality that great landholders constantly practised may not strike us today as consistent with the orderly management we tend to think inseparable from good economy. Even so, we must grant them at least this much thrift: they did not commonly spend their whole income. Part of their wool and raw hides they could usually sell for money. Some of that money they perhaps spent on the few objects of vanity and luxury the times could offer, but a good part of it they seem usually to have hoarded. In fact they could hardly do anything else with whatever money they saved. Trade was disgraceful to a gentleman, and lending money at interest, regarded then as usury and forbidden by law, would have been more disgraceful still. Besides, in those violent and disorderly times it was useful to keep a hoard of money on hand, so that if they were driven from their homes they would have something of known value to carry to a place of safety. The same violence that made hoarding convenient made concealing the hoard equally convenient. How often treasure-trove was found—buried treasure with no known owner—shows clearly how common both hoarding and concealing were in those times. Treasure-trove was then counted an important branch of the sovereign's revenue. Today, all the treasure-trove in the kingdom would scarcely make an important branch of the income of a single well-landed gentleman.

The same inclination to save and to hoard ran through the sovereign as well as his subjects. As I observed in the fourth book, among nations that know little of commerce and manufacturing, the sovereign is in a position that naturally pushes him toward the thrift accumulation requires. In that situation, even a sovereign's spending cannot be steered by the vanity that revels in the showy finery of a court. The ignorance of the age supplies few of the trinkets that such finery is made of. Standing armies are not yet needed, so even a sovereign, like any other great lord, can spend on almost nothing except gifts to his tenants and hospitality to his followers. But gifts and hospitality rarely lead to extravagance, whereas vanity almost always does. Accordingly, as already noted, all the ancient sovereigns of Europe had treasures. Every Tartar chief today is said to have one.

In a commercial country full of every kind of expensive luxury, the sovereign, like nearly all the great landowners in his realm, naturally spends much of his income buying those luxuries. His own country and its neighbours supply him generously with all the costly trinkets that make up the splendid but trivial display of a court. To put on an inferior display of the same sort, his nobles dismiss their followers, set their tenants free, and gradually become as insignificant as most of the wealthy townsmen in his dominions. The same frivolous passions that govern their conduct govern his. How could we suppose he would be the one rich man in his kingdom immune to pleasures of this kind? Even if he avoids what he is very likely to do—spending so much of his income on these pleasures that he badly weakens the state's defences—we can hardly expect him not to spend on them everything left over once those defences are paid for. His ordinary expense rises to equal his ordinary income, and it is well if it does not often exceed it. Accumulating treasure can no longer be expected, and when extraordinary emergencies demand extraordinary spending, he must necessarily ask his subjects for extraordinary help. The present and the late king of Prussia are the only great princes in Europe supposed to have built up any considerable treasure since the death of Henry IV of France in 1610. The thrift that leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republics as in monarchies. The Italian republics and the United Provinces of the Netherlands are all in debt. The canton of Berne is the one republic in Europe to have amassed any considerable treasure; the other Swiss republics have not. The taste for some kind of display—splendid buildings at least, and other public ornaments—often runs as strong in the seemingly sober senate-house of a small republic as in the dissolute court of the greatest king.

A lack of thrift in peacetime forces a state to take on debt in wartime. When war comes, the treasury holds no more money than is needed for the ordinary spending of the peacetime establishment. In war, an establishment three or four times that size becomes necessary to defend the state, and so a revenue three or four times the peacetime revenue is needed too. Suppose the sovereign had what he almost never has—an immediate way to raise his revenue in step with his expense; even then, the produce of the taxes that must supply this extra revenue would not start reaching the treasury until perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. But the moment war begins, or rather the moment it looks likely to begin, the army must be enlarged, the fleet fitted out, the garrison towns put in a state of defence; and that army, that fleet, those garrison towns must be supplied with arms, ammunition, and provisions. A huge, immediate expense must be met at that moment of immediate danger, and it cannot wait for the slow, gradual returns of new taxes. In this emergency, the government has no resource but borrowing.

The same commercial state of society that, through these moral causes, drives a government to borrow also gives its subjects both the means and the willingness to lend. If it usually brings the need to borrow, it likewise brings the ease of doing so.

A country full of merchants and manufacturers necessarily has a class of people through whose hands not only their own capital but also the capital of everyone who lends them money or trusts them with goods passes as often, or more often, than the income of a private man—who, having no trade or business, simply lives on his income—passes through his. Such a man's income can regularly pass through his hands only once a year. But the whole capital and credit of a merchant trading in goods that turn over quickly may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times in a year. A country full of merchants and manufacturers therefore necessarily has a class of people always in a position to advance, if they choose, a very large sum to the government. This is the source of the ability among the subjects of a commercial state to lend.

Commerce and manufacturing can rarely flourish for long in any state that lacks a steady administration of justice—where people do not feel secure in owning their property, where the law does not back the honouring of contracts, and where the state's authority is not reliably used to enforce payment of debts from everyone able to pay. In short, commerce and manufacturing can rarely flourish in any state without some degree of confidence in the government's justice. The same confidence that, in ordinary times, leads great merchants and manufacturers to trust their property to the protection of a particular government leads them, in extraordinary times, to trust that government with the use of their property. By lending money to the government, they do not for a moment reduce their ability to carry on their trade and manufactures; on the contrary, they usually increase it. The state's needs make the government, on most occasions, willing to borrow on terms extremely favourable to the lender. The security it grants the original creditor is made transferable to any other creditor, and because of the universal confidence in the state's justice it generally sells in the market for more than was first paid for it. So the merchant or moneyed man makes money by lending to the government and, instead of shrinking, enlarges his trading capital. He generally regards it as a favour, then, when the administration lets him take a share in the first subscription for a new loan. This is the source of the inclination, or willingness, among the subjects of a commercial state to lend.

A government of such a state is very apt to lean on this ability and willingness of its subjects to lend it money on extraordinary occasions. Foreseeing how easily it can borrow, it excuses itself from the duty of saving.

In a primitive state of society there are no great mercantile or manufacturing capitals. The individuals who hoard whatever money they can save, and conceal the hoard, do so out of distrust of the government's justice—out of fear that if it were known they had a hoard, and where to find it, they would soon be plundered. In such conditions, few people would be able, and nobody would be willing, to lend money to the government in extraordinary emergencies. The sovereign feels he must provide for such emergencies by saving, because he foresees that borrowing would be utterly impossible. This foresight strengthens his natural disposition to save still further.

The growth of the enormous debts that now oppress, and will probably in the long run ruin, all the great nations of Europe has followed a fairly uniform course. Nations, like private men, have generally begun by borrowing on what may be called personal credit, without assigning or mortgaging any particular fund to repay the debt; and when this resource failed them, they went on to borrow against assignments or mortgages of particular funds.

What is called the unfunded debt of Great Britain is contracted in the first of those two ways. It consists partly of a debt that bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest, resembling the debts a private man runs up on account; and partly of a debt that bears interest, resembling what a private man contracts on his bill or promissory note. Debts owed for extraordinary services, or for services either not budgeted for or not paid at the time they are performed—part of the extra costs of the army, navy, and ordnance, the arrears of subsidies to foreign princes, the arrears of seamen's wages, and so on—usually make up a debt of the first kind. Navy and exchequer bills, issued sometimes to pay part of such debts and sometimes for other purposes, make up a debt of the second kind: exchequer bills bearing interest from the day they are issued, and navy bills from six months after. The Bank of England keeps up the value of these bills and eases their circulation—either by voluntarily discounting them at their current value, or by agreeing with the government, for certain considerations, to circulate exchequer bills, that is, to accept them at par while paying any interest due on them—and so often enables the government to contract a very large debt of this kind. In France, where there is no bank, the state bills (billets d'état {See Examen des Reflexions Politiques sur les Finances.}) have sometimes sold at sixty and seventy per cent discount. During the great recoinage in King William's time, when the Bank of England chose to suspend its usual operations, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold at twenty-five to sixty per cent discount—owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed instability of the new government set up by the Revolution, but partly too to the lack of the Bank of England's support.

When this resource is exhausted and, in order to raise money, it becomes necessary to assign or mortgage some particular branch of the public revenue to repay the debt, the government has on different occasions done this in two different ways. Sometimes it has made the assignment or mortgage for a short period only—a year, or a few years, for example—and sometimes in perpetuity. In the first case, the fund was supposed sufficient to repay, within the set time, both the principal and the interest of the money borrowed. In the second, it was supposed sufficient to pay only the interest, or a perpetual annuity equal to the interest, with the government free to redeem this annuity at any time by repaying the principal borrowed. Money raised the first way was said to be raised by anticipation; raised the second way, by perpetual funding, or, more briefly, by funding.

In Great Britain, the annual land and malt taxes are regularly anticipated every year, by virtue of a borrowing clause permanently inserted into the acts that impose them. The Bank of England generally advances—at an interest that since the Revolution has ranged from eight to three per cent—the sums for which those taxes are granted, and receives repayment as their produce gradually comes in. If there is a shortfall, which there always is, it is covered out of the next year's supplies. So the only considerable branch of the public revenue still unmortgaged is regularly spent before it ever comes in. Like a thoughtless spendthrift whose pressing needs will not let him wait for the regular payment of his income, the state is constantly borrowing from its own agents and collectors and paying interest for the use of its own money.

In the reign of King William, and through much of Queen Anne's, before we had grown as familiar as we now are with perpetual funding, most new taxes were imposed for only a short term—four, five, six, or seven years—and much of each year's borrowing consisted of loans raised against the anticipated produce of those taxes. Since the produce was often not enough to repay the principal and interest within the set term, shortfalls arose; and to make them good it became necessary to prolong the term.

In 1697, by the 8th of William III, c. 20, the shortfalls of several taxes were charged on what was then called the first general mortgage or fund. This consisted of prolonging to 1 August 1706 several different taxes that would otherwise have expired sooner, whose produce was gathered into one general fund. The shortfalls charged on this prolonged term came to £5,160,459 14s 9½d.

In 1701, those duties, with some others, were prolonged still further for the same purposes, until 1 August 1710, and were called the second general mortgage or fund. The shortfalls charged on it came to £2,055,999 7s 11½d.
In 1707, those duties were prolonged still further, as a fund for new loans, until 1 August 1712, and were called the third general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed against it was £983,254 11s 9¼d.

In 1708, those duties were all continued still further (except the old subsidy of tonnage and poundage, of which only one half was made part of this fund, and a duty on the import of Scotch linen, which the Articles of Union had abolished), as a fund for new loans, until 1 August 1714, and were called the fourth general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed against it was £925,176 9s 2¼d.

In 1709, those duties were all continued still further (except the old subsidy of tonnage and poundage, now left out of this fund altogether), for the same purpose, until 1 August 1716, and were called the fifth general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed against it was £922,029 6s.
In 1710, those duties were prolonged again, until 1 August 1720, and were called the sixth general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed against it was £1,296,552 9s 11¾d.

In 1711, the same duties—by this point subject to four separate anticipations—together with several others, were continued for ever and made a fund for paying the interest on the capital of the South Sea Company, which that year had advanced to the government, to pay debts and make good shortfalls, the sum of £9,177,967 15s 4d, the largest loan ever made up to that time.

Before this, as far as I have been able to find, the chief—indeed the only—taxes imposed in perpetuity to pay the interest of a debt were those for paying the interest on the money the Bank and the East India Company had advanced to the government, and on what a projected land bank was expected to advance but never did. The Bank fund at this time came to £3,375,027 17s 10½d, on which was paid an annuity or interest of £206,501 15s 5d. The East India fund came to £3,200,000, on which was paid an annuity or interest of £160,000—the Bank fund at six per cent interest, the East India fund at five per cent.

In 1715, by the 1st of George I, c. 12, the various taxes that had been mortgaged to pay the Bank annuity, together with several others that this act likewise made perpetual, were gathered into one common fund, called the aggregate fund, which was charged not only with paying the Bank annuity but also with several other annuities and burdens of different kinds. This fund was later enlarged by the 3rd of George I, c. 8, and by the 5th of George I, c. 3, and the various duties then added to it were likewise made perpetual.

In 1717, by the 3rd of George I, c. 7, several other taxes were made perpetual and gathered into another common fund, called the general fund, to pay certain annuities amounting in all to £724,849 6s 10½d.

As a result of these various acts, most of the taxes that had previously been anticipated only for a short term of years were made perpetual, as a fund for paying not the principal but only the interest of the money that had been borrowed against them through successive anticipations.

Had money never been raised except by anticipation, a few years would have cleared the public revenue, requiring nothing of the government except that it not overload a fund by charging it with more debt than it could repay within the set term, and not anticipate a fund a second time before the first anticipation had expired. But most European governments have been incapable of even this much care. They have often overloaded a fund on the very first anticipation; and when they happened not to, they have generally made sure to overload it by anticipating it a second and a third time before the first anticipation expired. As the fund thus became wholly insufficient to repay both principal and interest of the money borrowed against it, it became necessary to charge it with the interest only, or a perpetual annuity equal to the interest; and such reckless anticipations inevitably gave rise to the more ruinous practice of perpetual funding. Though this practice necessarily pushes back the clearing of the public revenue from a fixed date to one so indefinite it is not likely ever to arrive, yet, because in every case a larger sum can be raised by this new method than by the old one of anticipation, the new method, once men have grown used to it, has in the state's great emergencies been universally preferred. Relieving the present emergency is always the chief concern of those directly in charge of public affairs. The future clearing of the public revenue they leave to posterity.

During Queen Anne's reign the market rate of interest had fallen from six to five per cent, and in the twelfth year of her reign five per cent was declared the highest rate that could lawfully be taken for money borrowed on private security. Soon after most of Great Britain's temporary taxes had been made perpetual and distributed among the aggregate, South Sea, and general funds, the public creditors, like those of private persons, were induced to accept five per cent interest on their money. This saved one per cent on the capital of most of the debts funded in perpetuity, or one-sixth of most of the annuities paid out of the three great funds just mentioned. This saving left a considerable surplus in the produce of the various taxes gathered into those funds, beyond what was needed to pay the annuities now charged on them, and laid the foundation of what has since been called the sinking fund. In 1717 it came to £523,454 7s 7½d. In 1727 the interest on most of the public debts was further reduced to four per cent, and in 1753 and 1757 to three and a half and three per cent—reductions that increased the sinking fund still further.

A sinking fund, though set up to repay old debts, makes contracting new ones much easier. It is a backup fund, always on hand, to be mortgaged in support of any doubtful fund against which money is to be raised in some emergency of the state. Whether Great Britain's sinking fund has more often been used for the one purpose or the other will become clear soon enough.

Besides these two methods of borrowing—by anticipation and by perpetual funding—there are two others that hold a sort of middle ground between them: borrowing on annuities for a term of years, and borrowing on annuities for lives.

During the reigns of King William and Queen Anne, large sums were often borrowed on annuities for terms of years, sometimes longer and sometimes shorter. In 1695 an act was passed to borrow one million on an annuity of fourteen per cent, or £140,000 a year, for sixteen years. In 1691 an act was passed to borrow a million on annuities for lives, on terms that would seem very advantageous today, but the subscription was not filled. The next year the shortfall was made good by borrowing on annuities for lives at fourteen per cent, a little more than seven years' purchase. In 1695 the people who had bought those annuities were allowed to exchange them for ninety-six-year annuities by paying sixty-three pounds in the hundred into the exchequer; that is, the difference between fourteen per cent for life and fourteen per cent for ninety-six years was sold for sixty-three pounds, or four and a half years' purchase. Such was the supposed instability of the government that even these terms found few buyers. In Queen Anne's reign, money was borrowed on various occasions both on annuities for lives and on annuities for terms of thirty-two, eighty-nine, ninety-eight, and ninety-nine years. In 1719 the holders of the thirty-two-year annuities were induced to accept, in their place, South Sea stock worth eleven and a half years' purchase of the annuities, together with an extra amount of stock equal to the arrears then due on them. In 1720 most of the other annuities for terms of years, both long and short, were subscribed into the same fund. The long annuities at that time came to £666,821 8s 3½d a year. On 5 January 1775 the remainder of them, or what had not been subscribed at that time, came to only £136,453 12s 8d.

During the two wars that began in 1739 and 1755, little money was borrowed either on annuities for terms of years or on annuities for lives. An annuity for ninety-eight or ninety-nine years, however, is worth nearly as much as a perpetuity, and one might therefore think it could raise nearly as much in loans. But those who buy into the public stocks in order to make family settlements and provide for the distant future would not want to buy into one whose value was steadily falling, and such people make up a very large share both of the holders and of the buyers of stock. So an annuity for a long term of years, though its intrinsic value may be very nearly that of a perpetual annuity, will not find nearly as many buyers. Subscribers to a new loan, who generally mean to sell their subscription as soon as they can, much prefer a perpetual annuity redeemable by Parliament to an irredeemable annuity for a long term of years of only equal amount. The value of the former may be supposed always the same, or very nearly so, and so it makes a more convenient transferable stock than the latter.

During those two wars, annuities, whether for terms of years or for lives, were seldom granted except as bonuses to subscribers of a new loan, over and above the redeemable annuity or interest on the strength of which the loan was supposed to be made. They were granted not as the proper fund against which the money was borrowed, but as an extra incentive to the lender.

Annuities for lives have occasionally been granted in two different ways: either on separate lives, or on groups of lives, which in French are called tontines, after their inventor. When annuities are granted on separate lives, the death of each individual annuitant relieves the public revenue of his annuity. When they are granted as tontines, the public revenue is not relieved at all until every annuitant in a group has died—a group that may sometimes consist of twenty or thirty people, the survivors inheriting the annuities of those who die before them, until the last survivor inherits the annuities of the whole group. On the same revenue, more money can always be raised by tontines than by annuities on separate lives. An annuity with a right of survivorship is really worth more than an equal annuity on a separate life; and, because of the confidence every man naturally has in his own good fortune—the very principle on which the success of all lotteries depends—such an annuity generally sells for somewhat more than it is worth. In countries where governments commonly raise money by granting annuities, tontines are therefore generally preferred to annuities on separate lives. The method that raises the most money is almost always preferred to the one most likely to clear the public revenue soonest.

In France a much larger share of the public debt consists of annuities for lives than in England. According to a memoir presented to the king by the parliament of Bordeaux in 1764, the whole public debt of France is estimated at 2,400 million livres, of which the capital for which life annuities had been granted is supposed to come to 300 million, an eighth of the whole public debt. The annuities themselves are reckoned at 30 million a year, a quarter of the 120 million that is the supposed interest on that whole debt. I know very well that these figures are not exact; but, having been presented by so respectable a body as approximations to the truth, they may, I think, be treated as such. The difference between the two governments' methods of borrowing is not caused by any difference in how anxious France and England are to clear the public revenue; it arises entirely from the different aims and interests of the lenders.

In England, where the seat of government is the greatest mercantile city in the world, the merchants are generally the people who advance money to the government. In advancing it, they do not mean to reduce their mercantile capital but, on the contrary, to increase it; and unless they expected to sell their share in the subscription for a new loan at some profit, they would never subscribe at all. But if, by advancing their money, they were to buy life annuities—whether on their own lives or on others'—instead of perpetual annuities, they would not always be so likely to sell them at a profit. Annuities on their own lives they would always sell at a loss, because no man will pay for an annuity on the life of another whose age and health are nearly his own the same price he would pay for one on his own life. An annuity on the life of a third person is, no doubt, of equal value to buyer and seller; but its real value begins to fall the moment it is granted and keeps falling, more and more, as long as it lasts. It can therefore never make as convenient a transferable stock as a perpetual annuity, whose real value may be supposed always the same, or very nearly so.

In France, where the seat of government is not a great mercantile city, merchants do not make up so large a share of the people who advance money to the government. The people involved in the finances—the farmers-general, the collectors of taxes not under farm, the court bankers, and so on—make up most of those who advance their money in public emergencies. Such people are commonly of low birth but great wealth, and often of great pride. They are too proud to marry their equals, and women of quality scorn to marry them. So they often decide to remain bachelors; and, having neither families of their own nor much regard for those of their relations—whom they are not always very keen to acknowledge—they want only to live in splendour during their own time, and are content for their fortune to end with them. Besides, the number of rich people who are either unwilling to marry, or whose way of life makes marrying improper or inconvenient, is much greater in France than in England. To such people, who care little or nothing for posterity, nothing could be more convenient than to exchange their capital for an income that lasts exactly as long as they wish it to, and no longer.

Since the ordinary peacetime expense of most modern governments equals, or nearly equals, their ordinary revenue, when war comes they are both unwilling and unable to raise their revenue in step with the rise in their expense. They are unwilling for fear of offending the people, who, faced with so great and sudden an increase in taxes, would soon turn against the war; and they are unable because they do not really know which taxes would be enough to produce the revenue needed. The ease of borrowing rescues them from the difficulty this fear and inability would otherwise cause. By borrowing, they can raise from year to year, with only a very moderate increase in taxes, enough money to carry on the war; and by perpetual funding they can raise the largest possible annual sum with the smallest possible increase in taxes. In great empires, the people who live in the capital and in provinces far from the fighting feel, many of them, scarcely any inconvenience from the war, but enjoy at their ease the entertainment of reading in the newspapers about the exploits of their own fleets and armies. For them, this entertainment makes up for the small difference between the taxes they pay because of the war and those they were used to paying in peacetime. They are commonly dissatisfied when peace returns, for it ends their entertainment and a thousand fanciful hopes of conquest and national glory that a longer war would have kept alive.

The return of peace, in fact, seldom frees them from most of the taxes imposed during the war. These are mortgaged to pay the interest on the debt contracted to carry it on. If, after paying the interest on this debt and covering the ordinary expense of government, the old revenue together with the new taxes yields some surplus, that surplus may perhaps be turned into a sinking fund to pay off the debt. But, first, this sinking fund—even supposing it were used for no other purpose—is generally quite inadequate to pay off, within any period for which peace can reasonably be expected to last, the whole debt contracted during the war; and, second, it is almost always used for other purposes.

The new taxes were imposed solely to pay the interest on the money borrowed against them. If they yield more, it is generally something neither intended nor expected, and therefore seldom very large. Sinking funds have generally arisen not so much from any surplus of the taxes over and above what was needed to pay the interest or annuity originally charged on them, as from a later reduction of that interest: those of Holland in 1655 and of the ecclesiastical state in 1685 were both formed this way. Hence the usual inadequacy of such funds.

Even in the deepest peace, various events occur that call for extraordinary spending; and the government always finds it more convenient to cover this spending by misusing the sinking fund than by imposing a new tax. Every new tax is felt at once, more or less, by the people. It always causes some grumbling and meets some opposition. The more taxes have already been multiplied, and the higher they have been raised on every taxable item, the more loudly the people complain of every new tax, and the harder it becomes either to find new things to tax or to raise the taxes already imposed on the old ones much higher. A momentary suspension of debt repayment is not felt at once by the people and causes neither grumbling nor complaint. Borrowing from the sinking fund is always an obvious, easy way out of the present difficulty. The more the public debts have piled up, the more necessary it becomes to work at reducing them, and the more dangerous and ruinous it is to misuse any part of the sinking fund—yet the less likely the public debt is to be reduced to any great degree, and the more surely the sinking fund is misused to cover all the extraordinary expenses that arise in peacetime. When a nation is already overburdened with taxes, nothing but the necessities of a new war—nothing but either the rage of national revenge or anxiety for national security—can induce the people to submit with any patience to a new tax. Hence the usual misuse of the sinking fund.

In Great Britain, ever since we first resorted to the ruinous expedient of perpetual funding, the reduction of the public debt in peacetime has never borne any proportion to its growth in wartime. It was in the war that began in 1668 and ended with the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697 that the foundation of Great Britain's present enormous debt was first laid.

On 31 December 1697 the public debts of Great Britain, funded and unfunded, came to £21,515,742 13s 8½d. A great part of these debts had been contracted on short anticipations, and some part on annuities for lives, so that before 31 December 1701—in less than four years—the sum of £5,121,041 12s 0¾d had been partly paid off and partly reverted to the public: a greater reduction of the public debt than has ever since been achieved in so short a time. The remaining debt therefore came to only £16,394,701 1s 7¼d.

In the war that began in 1702 and ended with the Treaty of Utrecht, the public debts grew still larger. On 31 December 1714 they came to £53,681,076 5s 6½d. Subscribing the short and long annuities into the South Sea fund increased the capital of the public debt, so that on 31 December 1722 it came to £55,282,978 1s 3⅚d. The reduction of the debt began in 1723 and went so slowly that by 31 December 1739, after seventeen years of deep peace, the whole sum paid off was no more than £8,328,554 17s 11³⁄₁₂d, the capital of the public debt then standing at £46,954,623 3s 4⁷⁄₁₂d.

The Spanish war, which began in 1739, and the French war that soon followed, caused a further increase in the debt, which on 31 December 1748, after the war had ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, came to £78,293,313 1s 10¾d. Seventeen years of the deepest peace had taken no more than £8,328,354 17s 11¼d off it. A war of less than nine years added £31,338,689 18s 6⅙d to it. {See James Postlethwaite's History of the Public Revenue.}

Under Mr Pelham's administration the interest on the public debt was reduced—or at least steps were taken to reduce it—from four to three per cent; the sinking fund was increased, and some of the public debt was paid off. In 1755, before the late war broke out, the funded debt of Great Britain came to £72,289,675. On 5 January 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, the funded debt came to £122,603,336 8s 2¼d. The unfunded debt has been put at £13,927,589 2s 2d. But the expense caused by the war did not end with the peace, so that although by 5 January 1764 the funded debt had risen (partly through a new loan and partly by funding part of the unfunded debt) to £129,586,789 10s 1¾d, there still remained—according to the well-informed author of Considerations on the Trade and Finances of Great Britain—an unfunded debt, brought to account in that year and the next, of £9,975,017 12s 2¹⁵⁄₄₄d. In 1764, therefore, the public debt of Great Britain, funded and unfunded together, came, according to this author, to £139,561,807 2s 4d. The life annuities, too, granted as bonuses to subscribers of the new loans in 1757, valued at fourteen years' purchase, were reckoned at £472,500; and the annuities for long terms of years, likewise granted as bonuses in 1761 and 1762, valued at twenty-seven and a half years' purchase, were reckoned at £6,826,875. During a peace of about seven years, the prudent and truly patriotic administration of Mr Pelham was unable to pay off an old debt of six million. During a war of nearly the same length, a new debt of more than seventy-five million was contracted.

On 5 January 1775 the funded debt of Great Britain came to £124,996,086 1s 6¼d, and the unfunded debt, apart from a large civil-list debt, to £4,150,236 3s 11⅞d—both together £129,146,322 5s 6d. By this account, the whole debt paid off during eleven years of deep peace came to only £10,415,476 16s 9⅞d. Even this small reduction, moreover, was not all made from savings out of the ordinary revenue of the state. Several outside sums, wholly independent of that ordinary revenue, contributed to it. Among these we may count an extra shilling in the pound land tax for three years, the two million received from the East India Company as compensation for their territorial acquisitions, and the £110,000 received from the Bank for renewing its charter. To these must be added several other sums which, since they arose out of the late war, ought perhaps to be treated as deductions from the cost of it. The chief are:
