What has been received from the sale of the ceded islands ......................... £95,500 0s 0d.

Add to this sum the balance of the Earl of Chatham's and Mr Calcraft's accounts, along with other army savings of the same kind, plus what has been received from the Bank, the East India Company, and the extra shilling-in-the-pound land tax, and the whole must come to a good deal more than five millions. So the debt that has been paid off since the peace out of the savings from the ordinary revenue of the state has not, taking one year with another, amounted to half a million a year. The sinking fund has certainly grown a good deal since the peace: the debt that has been paid off, the reduction of the redeemable four per cents to three per cents, and the life annuities that have fallen in have all added to it. If peace were to continue, perhaps a million a year might now be set aside from it towards discharging the debt. A second million was in fact paid during the past year; but at the same time a large civil-list debt was left unpaid, and we are now caught up in a new war that may, as it goes on, prove as costly as any of our earlier ones. {It has proved more expensive than any one of our former wars, and has saddled us with an additional debt of more than a hundred millions. During eleven years of deep peace, little more than ten millions of debt was paid off; during a seven-year war, more than a hundred millions was contracted.} The new debt that will probably be run up before the next campaign ends may come close to equalling all the old debt that has been paid off from savings out of the state's ordinary revenue. It is therefore pure fantasy to expect that the public debt will ever be completely paid off out of any savings likely to be made from that ordinary revenue as it now stands.

One author has portrayed the public funds of Europe's various indebted nations, and England's in particular, as a great pool of capital piled on top of the country's other capital—capital that supposedly extends its trade, multiplies its manufactures, and improves its land far beyond what the other capital alone could have achieved. He fails to see that the capital the public's first creditors lent to government was, from the moment he lent it, a definite portion of the annual produce diverted from acting as capital to acting as revenue: turned from maintaining productive workers to maintaining unproductive ones, and spent and wasted, usually within the year, with no prospect of any future reproduction. In return for the capital they advanced, the creditors did get an annuity from the public funds, in most cases worth rather more than what they had lent. This annuity certainly gave them back their capital and let them carry on their trade and business as fully as before, perhaps more so. In other words, it enabled them either to borrow fresh capital from other people on the security of the annuity, or, by selling it, to get from other people fresh capital of their own equal to or greater than what they had lent the government. But that new capital, which they bought or borrowed from others in this way, must already have existed in the country before, and must have been employed, as all capital is, in maintaining productive labour. When it passed into the hands of those who had lent their money to government, it was in some respects new capital to them, but it was not new to the country: it was only capital withdrawn from certain uses to be turned towards others. Though it replaced what they had lent the government, it did not replace it to the country. Had they not lent this capital to government, the country would have had two capitals—two portions of the annual produce—employed in maintaining productive labour instead of one.

When a revenue is raised within the year to cover the cost of government, drawn from free or unmortgaged taxes, all that happens is that a certain portion of private people's revenue is diverted from supporting one kind of unproductive labour to supporting another. Part of what they pay in those taxes might no doubt have been accumulated into capital and so used to maintain productive labour; but most of it would probably have been spent, and so used to maintain unproductive labour. Public spending paid for in this way does, more or less, hinder the further accumulation of new capital, but it does not necessarily destroy any capital that already exists.

When public spending is met by funding, it is met by the annual destruction of some capital that previously existed in the country—by diverting a portion of the annual produce that had been destined to maintain productive labour and using it instead to maintain unproductive labour. In this case, however, the taxes are lighter than they would have been if a revenue sufficient to cover the same spending had been raised within the year. So the private revenue of individuals is necessarily less burdened, and their ability to save and turn part of that revenue into capital is much less impaired. If funding destroys more old capital, it also hinders the accumulation or acquisition of new capital less than the method of paying for public spending out of a revenue raised within the year. Under funding, the thrift and industry of private people can more easily repair the holes that government waste and extravagance occasionally make in the general capital of society.

Yet funding has this advantage over the other system only while a war lasts. If the cost of war were always met by a revenue raised within the year, the taxes that supplied this extra revenue would last no longer than the war itself. Private people's ability to accumulate, though smaller during the war, would have been greater during peacetime than under funding. War would not necessarily destroy any old capital, and peace would build up far more new capital. Wars would generally be concluded more quickly and undertaken less recklessly. Feeling the full weight of a war while it lasted, the people would soon grow tired of it; and government, to keep them content, would not be obliged to carry it on any longer than necessary. The foreknowledge of the heavy and unavoidable burdens of war would stop people from recklessly demanding it when there was no real and solid interest to fight for. The periods in which private people's ability to accumulate was somewhat reduced would come round more rarely and last a shorter time, while the periods in which that ability was at its highest vigour would last far longer than they easily can under funding.

Besides, once funding has gone a certain way, the multiplication of taxes it brings sometimes impairs private people's ability to accumulate as much, even in peacetime, as the other system would in wartime. Great Britain's peacetime revenue now amounts to more than ten millions a year. If it were free and unmortgaged, it could, with proper management and without contracting a shilling of new debt, be enough to carry on the most vigorous war. As things are, the private revenue of Britain's inhabitants is as encumbered in peacetime, and their ability to accumulate as much impaired, as it would have been in the costliest war had the ruinous system of funding never been adopted.

It has been said that in paying the interest on the public debt, the right hand pays the left: the money does not leave the country, it is merely part of the revenue of one set of inhabitants transferred to another, and the nation is not a farthing poorer. This excuse rests entirely on the sophistry of the mercantile system, and after the long examination I have already given that system, perhaps nothing more need be said about it. It also assumes that the whole public debt is owed to the country's own inhabitants, which happens not to be true: the Dutch, along with several other foreign nations, hold a very considerable share of our public funds. But even if the whole debt were owed to the country's own inhabitants, that would not make it any less harmful.

Land and capital stock are the two original sources of all revenue, both private and public. Capital stock pays the wages of productive labour, whether employed in agriculture, manufactures, or commerce. The management of these two original sources of revenue belongs to two different sets of people: the proprietors of land, and the owners or employers of capital stock.

For the sake of his own revenue, the landowner has an interest in keeping his estate in the best condition he can—building and repairing his tenants' houses, making and maintaining the necessary drains and enclosures, and carrying out all those other costly improvements that are properly the landlord's to make and keep up. But various land taxes may cut his revenue so much, and various duties on the necessities and comforts of life may make that reduced revenue worth so little in real terms, that he finds himself simply unable to make or maintain these costly improvements. And once the landlord stops doing his part, it is altogether impossible for the tenant to keep doing his. As the landlord's distress grows, the country's agriculture must inevitably decline.

When various taxes on the necessities and comforts of life leave the owners and employers of capital stock finding that whatever revenue they get from it will not, in a particular country, buy the same quantity of those necessities and comforts that an equal revenue would buy almost anywhere else, they will be inclined to move elsewhere. And when, in order to collect those taxes, all or most merchants and manufacturers—that is, all or most of the employers of large capitals—come to be constantly exposed to the humiliating and harassing visits of the tax-gatherers, this inclination to move will soon turn into actual moving. The country's industry must inevitably fall away with the removal of the capital that supported it, and the ruin of trade and manufactures will follow the decline of agriculture.

To transfer the greater part of the revenue arising from land and capital stock—the two great sources of revenue—from those who own them and have a direct stake in the good condition of every particular plot of land and the good management of every particular portion of capital, to another set of people (the public's creditors, who have no such particular stake) must in the long run bring about both the neglect of land and the waste or removal of capital stock. A public creditor does, of course, have a general interest in the prosperity of the country's agriculture, manufactures, and commerce, and so in the good condition of its land and the good management of its capital stock. If there were any general failure or decline in any of these, the yield of the various taxes might no longer be enough to pay him the annuity or interest due to him. But a public creditor, considered simply as such, has no interest in the good condition of any particular plot of land or the good management of any particular portion of capital stock. As a public creditor, he has no knowledge of any such particular portion. He does not inspect it. He can take no care of it. Its ruin may in some cases be unknown to him, and cannot affect him directly.

The practice of funding has gradually weakened every state that has adopted it. The Italian republics seem to have started it. Genoa and Venice, the only two that can still claim an independent existence, have both been weakened by it. Spain seems to have learned the practice from the Italian republics, and—its taxes probably being less judicious than theirs—it has, relative to its natural strength, been weakened even more. Spain's debts go back a very long way: it was deeply in debt before the end of the sixteenth century, about a hundred years before England owed a shilling. France, for all its natural resources, languishes under an oppressive load of the same kind. The republic of the United Provinces is as weakened by its debts as either Genoa or Venice. Is it likely that in Great Britain alone a practice that has brought either weakness or dissolution to every other country should prove entirely harmless?

It may be said that the system of taxation in those various countries is inferior to England's. I believe it is. But it should be remembered that when even the wisest government has exhausted all the proper subjects of taxation, it must, in cases of urgent necessity, resort to improper ones. The wise republic of Holland has on some occasions been forced to resort to taxes as inconvenient as most of Spain's. Another war, begun before the public revenue had been significantly freed, and growing as costly as the last one, might, out of sheer necessity, make the British system of taxation as oppressive as that of Holland or even of Spain. To the credit of our present system of taxation, it has so far interfered so little with industry that, even through the costliest wars, the thrift and good conduct of individuals seem to have been able, by saving and accumulation, to repair every hole that government waste and extravagance had made in the general capital of society. At the end of the late war, the most expensive Great Britain ever waged, her agriculture was as flourishing, her manufacturers as numerous and as fully employed, and her commerce as extensive as they had ever been. The capital supporting all those branches of industry must therefore have been as great as it had ever been. Since the peace, agriculture has improved still further; house rents have risen in every town and village, a sign of the people's growing wealth and revenue; and the annual yield of most of the old taxes, the chief branches of excise and customs in particular, has kept rising—an equally clear sign of growing consumption, and so of growing produce, which alone could support that consumption. Great Britain seems to bear with ease a burden that half a century ago no one believed her capable of bearing. Let us not, however, rashly conclude from this that she can bear any burden whatever, nor even be too confident that she could bear, without great distress, a burden a little greater than the one already laid on her.

Once national debts have built up to a certain point, there is scarcely, I believe, a single instance of their having been fairly and completely paid off. The freeing of the public revenue, if it has ever been achieved at all, has always been achieved through bankruptcy—sometimes openly avowed, though often disguised as a pretended payment.

Raising the denomination of the coin has been the most common device for disguising a real public bankruptcy as a pretended payment. Suppose, for example, that an act of parliament or royal proclamation raised a sixpence to the denomination of a shilling, and twenty sixpences to that of a pound sterling. Then someone who under the old denomination had borrowed twenty shillings, or nearly four ounces of silver, would under the new one pay with twenty sixpences, or something less than two ounces. A national debt of about a hundred and twenty-eight millions, close to the total of Great Britain's funded and unfunded debt, could in this way be paid off with about sixty-four millions of our present money. It would, of course, be only a pretended payment, and the public's creditors would really be cheated of ten shillings in the pound of what was owed to them. The disaster would reach much further than the public's creditors, too: every private person's creditors would suffer a proportionate loss—and all this without any gain, but in most cases with a great additional loss, even to the public's creditors. If the public's creditors were themselves generally much in debt to others, they might in some degree offset their loss by paying their own creditors in the same debased coin in which the public had paid them. But in most countries the public's creditors are, for the most part, wealthy people who stand more as creditors than as debtors towards the rest of their fellow citizens. A pretended payment of this kind therefore usually aggravates, rather than relieves, the loss of the public's creditors, and, without any benefit to the public, spreads the disaster to a great many other innocent people. It causes a general and most ruinous overturning of private fortunes, in most cases enriching the idle and wasteful debtor at the expense of the industrious and thrifty creditor, and shifting a great part of the national capital from hands likely to increase and improve it to those likely to squander and destroy it. When a state finds it necessary to declare itself bankrupt, just as when an individual must do so, a fair, open, and avowed bankruptcy is always the course least dishonourable to the debtor and least harmful to the creditor. A state's honour is surely very poorly served when, to cover the disgrace of a real bankruptcy, it resorts to a juggling trick of this kind—so easily seen through, and at the same time so extremely harmful.

Almost all states, though, ancient as well as modern, when reduced to this necessity, have on some occasions played this very juggling trick. The Romans, at the end of the First Punic War, reduced the As—the coin or unit by which they reckoned the value of all their other coins—from containing twelve ounces of copper to containing only two; that is, they raised two ounces of copper to a denomination that had always before stood for the value of twelve. In this way the republic was able to pay the great debts it had contracted with a sixth of what it really owed. So sudden and so great a bankruptcy, we today would assume, must have provoked a very violent public outcry. It seems to have provoked none. The law that enacted it was, like all laws relating to the coin, introduced and carried through the popular assembly by a tribune, and was probably a very popular law. In Rome, as in all the other ancient republics, the poor were constantly in debt to the rich and the great, who, in order to secure their votes at the annual elections, used to lend them money at exorbitant interest; this, never being paid, soon piled up into a sum too large either for the debtor to pay or for anyone else to pay on his behalf. For fear of a very harsh execution, the debtor was obliged, without any further reward, to vote for whichever candidate his creditor recommended. Despite all the laws against bribery and corruption, the candidates' largesse, together with the occasional distributions of coin ordered by the senate, were the chief funds from which, in the later days of the Roman republic, the poorer citizens drew their subsistence. To free themselves from this subjection to their creditors, the poorer citizens were forever clamouring either for a total abolition of debts or for what they called new tables—that is, for a law entitling them to a full discharge on paying only a certain proportion of their accumulated debts. The law that reduced the coin of all denominations to a sixth of its former value, by letting them pay their debts with a sixth of what they really owed, was equivalent to the most advantageous new tables. To satisfy the people, the rich and the great were on several different occasions forced to consent to laws both abolishing debts and bringing in new tables; and they were probably induced to consent to this law partly for the same reason, and partly because, by freeing the public revenue, they could restore vigour to the government, of which they themselves were the chief directors. An operation of this kind would at a stroke reduce a debt of £128,000,000 to £21,333,333:6:8. During the Second Punic War, the As was reduced still further, first from two ounces of copper to one, and then from one ounce to half an ounce—that is, to a twenty-fourth of its original value. By combining the three Roman operations into one, a debt of a hundred and twenty-eight millions of our present money could in this way be cut all at once to a debt of £5,333,333:6:8. Even the enormous debt of Great Britain might in this way soon be paid off.

By such devices the coin of, I believe, every nation has been gradually reduced more and more below its original value, and the same nominal sum has gradually come to contain a smaller and smaller quantity of silver.

For the same purpose, nations have sometimes debased the standard of their coin—that is, mixed more alloy into it. If, for example, the pound weight of our silver coin contained eight ounces of alloy instead of the eighteen pennyweight of the present standard, then a pound sterling, or twenty shillings of such coin, would be worth little more than six shillings and eightpence of our present money. The quantity of silver in six shillings and eightpence of our present money would thus be raised almost to the denomination of a pound sterling. Debasing the standard has exactly the same effect as what the French call an augmentation, a direct raising of the denomination of the coin.

An augmentation, or direct raising of the coin's denomination, always is, and by its nature must be, an open and avowed operation. By it, pieces of smaller weight and bulk are called by the same name previously given to pieces of greater weight and bulk. Debasing the standard, by contrast, has generally been a concealed operation. By it, pieces are issued from the mint of the same denomination and, as nearly as could be arranged, of the same weight, bulk, and appearance as pieces already in circulation of much greater value. When King John of France, {See Du Cange, Glossary, under Moneta; the Benedictine edition.} debased his coin in order to pay his debts, all the officers of his mint were sworn to secrecy. Both operations are unjust. But a simple augmentation is an injustice of open violence, whereas a debasement is an injustice of treacherous fraud. So this latter operation, once discovered—and it could never be hidden very long—has always stirred up far greater indignation than the former. After any considerable augmentation, the coin has very seldom been brought back to its former weight; but after the greatest debasements, it has almost always been brought back to its former fineness. Hardly ever has anything else been able to appease the fury and indignation of the people.

Towards the end of Henry VIII's reign, and at the beginning of Edward VI's, the English coin was not only raised in its denomination but debased in its standard. The same frauds were committed in Scotland during the minority of James VI. They have occasionally been committed in most other countries as well.

To expect that the public revenue of Great Britain can ever be completely freed—or even that any considerable progress can be made towards freeing it—while the surplus of that revenue (what is left over after paying the annual cost of the peace establishment) is so very small, seems altogether vain. That liberation clearly can never come about without either a very considerable increase in the public revenue or an equally considerable cut in public spending.

A more equal land tax, a more equal tax on house rents, and such changes to the present system of customs and excise as I mentioned in the previous chapter, might perhaps—without increasing the burden on most of the people, but only spreading its weight more equally over the whole—produce a considerable increase in revenue. Even the most sanguine projector, however, could scarcely flatter himself that any increase of this kind would give any reasonable hope either of freeing the public revenue altogether or even of making enough progress towards that in peacetime to prevent or offset the further build-up of public debt in the next war.

By extending the British system of taxation to all the different provinces of the empire inhabited by people of British or European descent, a much greater increase in revenue might be expected. This, however, could hardly be done in keeping with the principles of the British constitution without admitting into the British parliament—or, if you like, into the states-general of the British empire—a fair and equal representation of all those provinces, each province's representation bearing the same proportion to the yield of its taxes as Great Britain's representation bears to the yield of the taxes levied on Great Britain. The private interest of many powerful individuals and the entrenched prejudices of large bodies of people do seem, at present, to set up against so great a change obstacles that may be very hard, perhaps altogether impossible, to overcome. Without claiming to settle whether such a union is practicable or not, however, it may not be out of place, in a speculative work of this kind, to consider how far the British system of taxation might be applied to all the different provinces of the empire; what revenue might be expected from it if so applied; and how a general union of this kind might affect the happiness and prosperity of the various provinces it took in. Such speculation can, at worst, be regarded only as a new Utopia—less entertaining, certainly, but no more useless and fanciful than the old one.
The land tax, the stamp duties, and the various duties of customs and excise make up the four chief branches of British taxation.

Ireland is certainly as able, and our American and West Indian plantations more able, to pay a land tax than Great Britain. Where the landlord is subject to neither tithe nor poor-rate, he must certainly be more able to pay such a tax than where he is subject to both those other burdens. The tithe, where there is no modus and it is levied in kind, cuts into what would otherwise be the landlord's rent more than a land tax really amounting to five shillings in the pound. Such a tithe will be found, in most cases, to come to more than a fourth of the real rent of the land—of what remains after fully replacing the farmer's capital together with his reasonable profit. If all moduses and all impropriations were done away with, the full church tithe of Great Britain and Ireland could hardly be reckoned at less than six or seven millions. If there were no tithe in either Great Britain or Ireland, the landlords could afford to pay six or seven millions in additional land tax without being more burdened than a very large part of them already are. America pays no tithe, and could therefore very well afford to pay a land tax. The lands in America and the West Indies, it is true, are generally not tenanted or leased out to farmers, so they could not be assessed by any rent roll. But neither were the lands of Great Britain, in the fourth year of William and Mary, assessed by any rent roll; they were assessed by a very loose and inaccurate estimate. The lands in America might be assessed either the same way, or by an equitable valuation based on an accurate survey, like the one recently carried out in the Milanese and in the dominions of Austria, Prussia, and Sardinia.

Stamp duties, clearly, could be levied without any change in all countries where the forms of legal process, and the deeds by which property—both real and personal—is transferred, are the same, or nearly the same.

Extending Great Britain's customs-house laws to Ireland and the plantations, provided it were accompanied, as in justice it ought to be, with an extension of free trade, would be in the highest degree advantageous to both. All the invidious restraints that now oppress the trade of Ireland, and the distinction between America's enumerated and non-enumerated commodities, would be entirely at an end. The countries north of Cape Finisterre would be as open to every part of America's produce as those south of that cape now are to some parts of it. Thanks to this uniformity in the customs-house laws, the trade between all the different parts of the British empire would be as free as Great Britain's coasting trade now is. The British empire would thus offer, within itself, an immense internal market for every part of the produce of all its various provinces. So great an enlargement of the market would soon make up, to both Ireland and the plantations, for anything they might suffer from the increase in customs duties.

The excise is the only part of the British system of taxation that would need to be varied at all, depending on which province of the empire it was applied to. It could be applied to Ireland without any change, since that kingdom's produce and consumption are exactly the same in nature as Great Britain's. In its application to America and the West Indies, whose produce and consumption are so very different from Great Britain's, some modification might be needed, just as in its application to the cider and beer counties of England.

A fermented drink, for instance, that is called beer but, being made from molasses, bears very little resemblance to ours, makes up a considerable part of the common drink of the people in America. Since this liquor will keep only for a few days, it cannot, like our beer, be brewed and stored for sale in great breweries; every private family must brew it for their own use, just as they cook their food. But to subject every private family to the odious visits and inspections of the tax-gatherers, as we subject the keepers of ale-houses and the brewers who brew for public sale, would be altogether incompatible with liberty. If, for the sake of equality, it were thought necessary to tax this liquor, it might be taxed by taxing the material it is made from, either at the place of manufacture or—if the circumstances of the trade made such an excise unsuitable—by laying a duty on its import into the colony where it was to be consumed. Besides the duty of one penny a gallon imposed by the British parliament on the import of molasses into America, there is a provincial tax of this kind on their import into Massachusetts Bay, in ships belonging to any other colony, of eightpence the hogshead, and another on their import from the northern colonies into South Carolina, of fivepence the gallon. Or, if neither of these methods proved convenient, each family might compound for its consumption of this liquor—either according to the number of persons it contained, in the same way that private families compound for the malt tax in England; or according to the different ages and sexes of those persons, in the same way that several different taxes are levied in Holland; or, more or less as Sir Matthew Decker proposes that all taxes on consumable goods should be levied in England. This mode of taxation, as already noted, is not very convenient when applied to things consumed quickly. It might, however, be adopted in cases where nothing better could be done.

Sugar, rum, and tobacco are commodities that are nowhere necessities of life, that have become objects of almost universal consumption, and that are therefore extremely suitable subjects of taxation. If a union with the colonies took place, those commodities might be taxed either before they left the hands of the maker or grower; or, if that mode of taxation did not suit those people's circumstances, they might be deposited in public warehouses—both at the place of manufacture and at all the various ports of the empire to which they might later be carried—to remain there, under the joint custody of the owner and the revenue officer, until they were delivered out, either to the consumer, to the retail merchant for home consumption, or to the merchant-exporter; the tax not falling due until that delivery. When delivered out for export, they would go duty-free, on proper security being given that they really would be exported out of the empire. These are perhaps the chief commodities for which a union with the colonies might call for any considerable change in the present system of British taxation.

What revenue this system of taxation, extended to all the various provinces of the empire, might yield is of course altogether impossible to estimate with any tolerable exactness. By means of this system, more than ten millions of revenue is raised annually in Great Britain from fewer than eight millions of people. Ireland contains more than two millions of people, and, according to the accounts laid before the Congress, the twelve associated provinces of America contain more than three. Those accounts, however, may have been exaggerated, perhaps to encourage their own people or to intimidate ours; so let us suppose that our North American and West Indian colonies together contain no more than three millions, and that the whole British empire, in Europe and America, contains no more than thirteen millions of inhabitants. If, on fewer than eight millions of inhabitants, this system of taxation raises a revenue of more than ten millions sterling, then on thirteen millions of inhabitants it ought to raise a revenue of more than sixteen millions two hundred and fifty thousand pounds sterling. From this revenue, supposing the system could produce it, must be deducted the revenue usually raised in Ireland and the plantations to cover the cost of their respective civil governments. The cost of Ireland's civil and military establishment, together with the interest on its public debt, came on average over the two years ending March 1775 to something under seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds a year. By a very exact account, the revenue of the chief colonies of America and the West Indies came, before the start of the present disturbances, to a hundred and forty-one thousand eight hundred pounds. This account, however, leaves out the revenue of Maryland, of North Carolina, and of all our late acquisitions, both on the continent and in the islands, which may make a difference of thirty or forty thousand pounds. For round numbers, then, let us suppose that the revenue needed to support the civil government of Ireland and the plantations comes to a million. That would leave a revenue of fifteen millions two hundred and fifty thousand pounds to be applied towards the general expense of the empire and towards paying off the public debt. But if a million could be spared in peacetime from the present revenue of Great Britain towards paying that debt, then six millions two hundred and fifty thousand pounds could very well be spared from this improved revenue. This great sinking fund could also be increased every year by the interest on the debt discharged the year before, and might in this way grow so rapidly as to be enough within a few years to discharge the whole debt, and so completely restore the empire's now weakened and flagging vigour. Meanwhile the people might be relieved of some of the most burdensome taxes—those laid either on the necessities of life or on the materials of manufacture. The labouring poor would thus be able to live better, to work more cheaply, and to send their goods to market more cheaply. The cheapness of their goods would increase the demand for them, and so for the labour of those who produced them. This rise in the demand for labour would both increase the numbers and improve the circumstances of the labouring poor. Their consumption would grow, and with it the revenue arising from all those articles of their consumption on which the taxes were allowed to remain.

The revenue arising from this system of taxation, however, might not increase straight away in proportion to the number of people subjected to it. Great indulgence would for some time be owed to those provinces of the empire newly subjected to burdens they had not been used to before; and even once the same taxes came to be levied everywhere as exactly as possible, they would not everywhere yield a revenue proportioned to the number of people. In a poor country, the consumption of the chief commodities subject to customs and excise duties is very small, and in a thinly populated country the opportunities for smuggling are very great. The consumption of malt liquors among the lower ranks of people in Scotland is very small, and the excise on malt, beer, and ale yields less there than in England, relative to the number of people and the rate of duty, which on malt is different on account of a supposed difference in quality. In these particular branches of the excise there is not, I think, much more smuggling in the one country than in the other. The duties on the distillery, and most of the customs duties, yield less in Scotland than in England relative to the number of people, not only because less of the taxed commodities is consumed, but also because smuggling is so much easier. In Ireland the lower ranks of people are still poorer than in Scotland, and many parts of the country are almost as thinly populated. In Ireland, therefore, the consumption of the taxed commodities relative to the number of people might be still smaller than in Scotland, with smuggling about as easy. In America and the West Indies, the white people, even of the lowest rank, are in much better circumstances than those of the same rank in England, and their consumption of all the luxuries they usually indulge in is probably much greater. The blacks, who make up the greater part of the inhabitants both of the southern mainland colonies and of the West Indian islands, are in a state of slavery and so are no doubt in a worse condition than the poorest people in either Scotland or Ireland. We must not, however, imagine on that account that they are worse fed, or that their consumption of articles that might bear moderate duties is less than that even of the lower ranks of people in England. So that they may work well, it is in their master's interest to feed them well and keep them in good heart, just as it is in his interest that his working cattle should be so. The blacks accordingly have almost everywhere their allowance of rum and of molasses or spruce-beer, just as the white servants do, and this allowance would probably not be withdrawn even if those articles were made subject to moderate duties. The consumption of the taxed commodities relative to the number of inhabitants would therefore probably be as great in America and the West Indies as in any part of the British empire. The opportunities for smuggling, however, would be much greater, America being, relative to the extent of the country, far more thinly populated than either Scotland or Ireland. But if the revenue now raised by the various duties on malt and malt liquors were levied by a single duty on malt, the chance of smuggling in the most important branch of the excise would be almost entirely removed; and if the customs duties, instead of being imposed on almost every article of import, were confined to a few of the most general use and consumption, and if the levying of those duties were brought under the excise laws, the chance of smuggling, though not so completely removed, would be very much reduced. As a result of these two apparently very simple and easy changes, the customs and excise duties might probably yield a revenue as great, relative to the consumption of the most thinly populated province, as they now do relative to that of the most populous.

The Americans, it has been said, have no gold or silver money, since the country's internal trade is carried on by a paper currency, and whatever gold and silver occasionally reaches them is all sent to Great Britain in payment for the goods they get from us. But without gold and silver, it is added, taxes cannot possibly be paid. We already take all the gold and silver they have. How can we draw from them what they do not have?

The present scarcity of gold and silver money in America is not the result of that country's poverty, or of the people's inability to buy those metals. In a country where the wages of labour are so much higher and the price of provisions so much lower than in England, the bulk of the people must surely have the means to buy a greater quantity, if it were either necessary or convenient for them to do so. The scarcity of those metals, then, must be the result of choice, not of necessity.
Gold or silver money is necessary or convenient only for transacting business, whether at home or abroad.

The domestic business of every country, as was shown in the second book of this Inquiry, can—at least in peacetime—be carried on by means of a paper currency with nearly the same convenience as by gold and silver money. It suits the Americans, who could always employ profitably in improving their lands a greater stock than they can easily come by, to save as much as possible the cost of so expensive an instrument of commerce as gold and silver, and to use instead the part of their surplus produce that would be needed to buy those metals to buy the tools of trade, the materials of clothing, various parts of household furniture, and the ironwork needed to build and extend their settlements and plantations—to buy not dead stock, but active and productive stock. The colony governments find it in their interest to supply the people with a quantity of paper money fully sufficient, and generally more than sufficient, for carrying on their domestic business. Some of those governments—Pennsylvania's in particular—draw a revenue from lending this paper money to their subjects at so much per cent interest. Others, like that of Massachusetts Bay, issue a paper money of this kind on extraordinary emergencies to meet public spending, and afterwards, when it suits the colony, redeem it at the depreciated value to which it gradually falls. In 1747, {See Hutchinson's History of Massachusetts Bay, vol. ii, page 436 and following.} that colony paid off in this way most of its public debts, with a tenth of the money for which its bills had been issued. It suits the planters to save the cost of employing gold and silver money in their domestic dealings, and it suits the colony governments to supply them with a medium that, though it has some very considerable disadvantages, lets them save that cost. The flood of paper money necessarily drives gold and silver out of the colonies' domestic dealings, for the same reason it has driven those metals out of most of the domestic dealings in Scotland; and in both countries it is not poverty but the enterprising and projecting spirit of the people, their wish to employ all the stock they can get as active and productive stock, that has caused this flood of paper money.

In the foreign trade that the various colonies carry on with Great Britain, gold and silver are used more or less exactly in proportion as they are more or less necessary. Where those metals are not necessary, they seldom appear. Where they are necessary, they are generally found.

In the trade between Great Britain and the tobacco colonies, British goods are generally supplied to the colonists on a fairly long credit, and afterwards paid for in tobacco, valued at a certain price. It is more convenient for the colonists to pay in tobacco than in gold and silver. It would be more convenient for any merchant to pay for the goods his correspondents have sold him in some other kind of goods he happens to deal in than in money. Such a merchant would have no need to keep any part of his stock idle and in ready cash to meet occasional demands. He could at all times hold a larger quantity of goods in his shop or warehouse, and could trade on a larger scale. But it seldom happens to suit all of a merchant's correspondents to receive payment for the goods they sell him in goods of some other kind that he happens to deal in. The British merchants who trade to Virginia and Maryland happen to be a particular set of correspondents who find it more convenient to receive payment for the goods they sell those colonies in tobacco than in gold and silver. They expect to make a profit by selling the tobacco; they could make none by selling the gold and silver. Gold and silver, therefore, very seldom appear in the trade between Great Britain and the tobacco colonies. Maryland and Virginia have as little need of those metals in their foreign as in their domestic trade. They are accordingly said to have less gold and silver money than any other colonies in America. Yet they are reckoned as thriving, and so as rich, as any of their neighbours.

In the northern colonies—Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, the four governments of New England, and so on—the value of their own produce that they export to Great Britain is less than that of the manufactures they import for their own use and for some of the other colonies, for which they act as carriers. A balance must therefore be paid to the mother country in gold and silver, and this balance they generally find.

In the sugar colonies, the value of the produce annually exported to Great Britain is much greater than that of all the goods imported from there. If the sugar and rum sent to the mother country each year were paid for in those colonies, Great Britain would have to send out a very large balance in money every year, and a certain kind of politician would regard the West India trade as extremely disadvantageous. But it so happens that many of the chief owners of the sugar plantations live in Great Britain. Their rents are remitted to them in sugar and rum, the produce of their estates. The sugar and rum that the West India merchants buy in those colonies on their own account are not equal in value to the goods they sell there each year. A balance must therefore be paid to them in gold and silver, and this balance, too, is generally found.

The difficulty and irregularity of payment from the various colonies to Great Britain have not been at all in proportion to the largeness or smallness of the balances respectively due from them. Payments have generally been more regular from the northern colonies than from the tobacco colonies, even though the former have generally paid a fairly large balance in money while the latter have paid either no balance or a much smaller one. The difficulty of getting payment from our various sugar colonies has been greater or less in proportion not so much to the size of the balances due from them as to the amount of uncultivated land they contained—that is, to the greater or smaller temptation the planters were under to over-trade, or to undertake the settlement and planting of more waste land than their capitals could stretch to. The returns from the great island of Jamaica, where there is still much uncultivated land, have on this account generally been more irregular and uncertain than those from the smaller islands of Barbados, Antigua, and St Christopher's, which have for many years been fully cultivated and have on that account left less scope for the planter's speculations. The new acquisitions of Grenada, Tobago, St Vincent's, and Dominica have opened a fresh field for speculations of this kind, and the returns from those islands have lately been as irregular and uncertain as those from the great island of Jamaica.

It is not, then, the poverty of the colonies that causes, in most of them, the present scarcity of gold and silver money. Their great demand for active and productive stock makes it convenient for them to hold as little dead stock as possible, and so disposes them to make do with a cheaper, though less convenient, instrument of commerce than gold and silver. They are thereby able to turn the value of that gold and silver into the tools of trade, the materials of clothing, household furniture, and the ironwork needed to build and extend their settlements and plantations. In those lines of business that cannot be carried on without gold and silver money, it appears that they can always find the necessary quantity of those metals; and if they often do not find it, their failure is generally the result not of any necessary poverty but of their unnecessary and excessive enterprise. It is not because they are poor that their payments are irregular and uncertain, but because they are too eager to grow excessively rich. Even if all that part of the colony taxes' produce which was over and above what was needed to cover the cost of their own civil and military establishments were to be remitted to Great Britain in gold and silver, the colonies have plenty with which to buy the required quantity of those metals. They would in that case be obliged, it is true, to exchange part of their surplus produce—with which they now buy active and productive stock—for dead stock. In carrying on their domestic business they would have to use a costly instead of a cheap instrument of commerce, and the cost of buying this costly instrument might somewhat dampen the liveliness and ardour of their excessive enterprise in improving land. It might not, however, be necessary to remit any part of the American revenue in gold and silver. It might be remitted in bills drawn on, and accepted by, particular merchants or companies in Great Britain to whom part of America's surplus produce had been consigned, who would pay the American revenue into the treasury in money after having themselves received its value in goods; and the whole business might often be carried out without exporting a single ounce of gold or silver from America.

It is not contrary to justice that both Ireland and America should contribute towards discharging the public debt of Great Britain. That debt was contracted in support of the government established by the Revolution—a government to which the Protestants of Ireland owe not only all the authority they now enjoy in their own country but every security they have for their liberty, their property, and their religion; a government to which several of the American colonies owe their present charters, and so their present constitution, and to which all the American colonies owe the liberty, security, and property they have enjoyed ever since. That public debt was contracted in defence not of Great Britain alone but of all the various provinces of the empire. The immense debt contracted in the late war in particular, and a great part of that contracted in the war before, were both properly contracted in defence of America.

By a union with Great Britain, Ireland would gain, besides free trade, other advantages far more important, which would much more than make up for any increase in taxes that came with the union. By the union with England, the middling and lower ranks of people in Scotland gained a complete deliverance from the power of an aristocracy that had always oppressed them. By a union with Great Britain, most people of all ranks in Ireland would gain an equally complete deliverance from a far more oppressive aristocracy—an aristocracy founded not, like that of Scotland, on the natural and respectable distinctions of birth and fortune, but on the most odious of all distinctions, those of religious and political prejudice; distinctions that, more than any other, fire both the insolence of the oppressors and the hatred and indignation of the oppressed, and that commonly make the inhabitants of the same country more hostile to one another than the inhabitants of different countries ever are. Without a union with Great Britain, the inhabitants of Ireland are not likely, for many ages, to think of themselves as one people.

No oppressive aristocracy has ever prevailed in the colonies. Even they, however, would gain considerably in happiness and tranquillity by a union with Great Britain. It would at least free them from those rancorous and virulent factions that are inseparable from small democracies, and that have so often divided the affections of their people and disturbed the peace of their governments, so nearly democratic in form. In the event of a total separation from Great Britain—which, unless prevented by a union of this kind, seems very likely to happen—those factions would be ten times more virulent than ever. Before the present disturbances began, the coercive power of the mother country had always been able to keep those factions from breaking out into anything worse than gross brutality and insult. If that coercive power were entirely removed, they would probably soon break out into open violence and bloodshed. In all large countries united under one uniform government, the spirit of party commonly prevails less in the remote provinces than at the centre of the empire. The distance of those provinces from the capital, the chief seat of the great scramble of faction and ambition, makes them enter less into the views of any of the contending parties, and makes them more indifferent and impartial spectators of the conduct of all. The spirit of party prevails less in Scotland than in England. In the event of a union, it would probably prevail less in Ireland than in Scotland, and the colonies would probably soon enjoy a degree of concord and unanimity unknown at present in any part of the British empire. Both Ireland and the colonies, it is true, would be subject to heavier taxes than any they now pay. But thanks to a diligent and faithful application of the public revenue towards discharging the national debt, most of those taxes might not last long, and the public revenue of Great Britain might soon be brought down to what was needed to keep up a moderate peace establishment.

The territorial acquisitions of the East India Company—the undoubted right of the Crown, that is, of the state and people of Great Britain—might be turned into another source of revenue, more abundant perhaps than all those already mentioned. Those countries are described as more fertile, more extensive, and, relative to their extent, much richer and more populous than Great Britain. To draw a great revenue from them, it would probably not be necessary to introduce any new system of taxation into countries already sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, taxed. It might perhaps be more fitting to lighten than to add to the burden of those unfortunate countries, and to try to draw a revenue from them not by imposing new taxes but by preventing the embezzlement and misapplication of most of those they already pay.

If it should turn out to be impracticable for Great Britain to draw any considerable increase of revenue from any of the resources mentioned above, the only resource left to her is to cut her spending. In both the collecting and the spending of the public revenue, though there may still be room for improvement in each, Great Britain seems to be at least as economical as any of her neighbours. The military establishment she keeps up for her own defence in peacetime is more moderate than that of any European state that can claim to rival her in either wealth or power. None of these items, then, seems to allow any considerable cut in spending. The cost of the colonies' peace establishment was, before the present disturbances began, very considerable, and is a cost that may, and—if no revenue can be drawn from them—certainly ought to be, saved altogether. This constant peacetime cost, though very great, is trifling compared with what defending the colonies has cost us in wartime. The last war, undertaken entirely on account of the colonies, cost Great Britain, as already noted, upwards of ninety millions. The Spanish war of 1739 was chiefly undertaken on their account, and in it, and in the French war that followed from it, Great Britain spent upwards of forty millions, a great part of which ought justly to be charged to the colonies. In those two wars the colonies cost Great Britain much more than double the sum the national debt amounted to before the first of them began. Had it not been for those wars, that debt might, and probably would, by now have been completely paid off; and had it not been for the colonies, the former of those wars might not, and the latter certainly would not, have been undertaken. It was because the colonies were supposed to be provinces of the British empire that this expense was laid out on them. But countries that contribute neither revenue nor military force towards the support of the empire cannot be considered provinces. They may perhaps be considered appendages, a sort of splendid and showy equipage of the empire. But if the empire can no longer bear the cost of keeping up this equipage, it surely ought to lay it down; and if it cannot raise its revenue in proportion to its expense, it ought at least to fit its expense to its revenue. If the colonies, despite their refusal to submit to British taxes, are still to be regarded as provinces of the British empire, their defence in some future war may cost Great Britain as great an expense as it ever has in any former war. For more than a century, the rulers of Great Britain have amused the people with the fancy that they possessed a great empire on the west side of the Atlantic. This empire, however, has so far existed in imagination only. It has so far been not an empire but the project of an empire, not a gold mine but the project of a gold mine—a project that has cost, that continues to cost, and that, if pursued in the same way as before, is likely to cost immense expense without being likely to bring any profit; for the effects of the monopoly of the colony trade, as has been shown, are to the great body of the people mere loss instead of profit. It is surely now time that our rulers either made this golden dream real—the dream in which they, and perhaps the people too, have been indulging—or else awoke from it themselves and tried to wake the people. If the project cannot be completed, it ought to be given up. If any of the provinces of the British empire cannot be made to contribute towards supporting the whole empire, it is surely time that Great Britain freed herself from the expense of defending those provinces in wartime, and of supporting any part of their civil or military establishment in peacetime, and tried to fit her future views and designs to the real mediocrity of her circumstances.
